prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "SASOL LTD" (ticker SSL), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "SSL", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Sasol Limited
result.industry: Integrated energy and chemicals (coal/gas-to-liquids fuels and commodity/specialty chemicals)
markets: South African liquid fuels (petrol, diesel, jet fuel) – retail, commercial and wholesale
Base chemicals (polymers, solvents, fertilisers and explosives) in South Africa and the US
Differentiated/specialty chemicals (alcohols, surfactants, waxes, alumina) in the US, Europe and Asia
Natural gas supply to South African industry from Mozambique
Coal mining (largely captive supply to Secunda)

mission.source: Sasol website, 'Purpose and Values' page (published as Sasol's purpose)
mission.plain: Sasol says it wants to use new ideas and technology to make energy and chemicals in ways that help the world.

about.plain: Sasol is a big South African company that turns coal and natural gas into fuels like petrol and diesel, using a special chemical process. It also makes lots of chemicals that other factories use to make plastics, soaps, cleaning products and fertilisers. Its giant plant at Secunda is one of the largest fuel-and-chemical factories in the world. It sells its chemicals in Africa, America, Europe and Asia.
about.customers: Drivers at its filling stations, mines, farms, airlines and transport firms that buy fuel, and factories around the world that buy its chemicals.
about.everyday: The petrol in many South African cars and ingredients in everyday soaps, shampoos and plastic packaging can come from Sasol.

money.plain: petrol, diesel and jet fuel sold mainly in South Africa
plastics, solvents, fertiliser and explosives made in South Africa
specialty chemicals for soaps, cosmetics and industry made in Europe and Asia
chemicals and plastics made at Lake Charles in the US
natural gas piped from Mozambique to South African factories

money.part: Sustainable fuels (Sasol ecoFT, green hydrogen, sustainable aviation fuel)
money.plain: low-carbon fuels made with its Fischer-Tropsch know-how

result.summary: Sasol has a narrow, asset-based advantage: its Secunda coal-to-liquids complex, captive coal mines, Mozambican gas and decades of proprietary Fischer-Tropsch know-how give it a hard-to-replicate integrated position in South Africa. But its products are commodities priced off oil and chemical markets, its returns have been erratic (an R75.4bn remeasurement charge and a net loss in FY2024, R16.8bn of impairments in FY2026), and carbon rules and declining Mozambican gas weaken the position over time.

pricingPower.evidence: Fuel prices in South Africa are set off the regulated, import-parity basic fuel price and Brent, and chemicals are priced off global commodity markets; FY2026 turnover rose 9.2% to R272,118m mainly because average Brent rose 7% to US$79.47/bbl and refining margins more than doubled, not because of Sasol's own pricing decisions, while a 7% stronger rand and weaker chemical prices hurt.

moats.evidence: Sasol is a well-known name in South Africa through its fuel stations, but fuels and base chemicals are bought on price and specification, not brand.
Some South African industrial gas customers depend on Sasol's pipeline gas from Mozambique (55.3 bscf sold in South Africa in FY2026), but fuel and most chemical buyers can switch suppliers easily.
Selling fuels and chemicals creates no network effect.

Secunda is one of the world's largest synthetic fuel and chemicals sites, integrated from its own coal to fuels and chemicals; Sasol says its Secunda oil break-even fell to US$49/bbl in FY2026 after production rose 8% to 7.26 mt.

Its inland South African plants (Secunda, Sasolburg and the Natref refinery joint venture with TotalEnergies) and the gas pipeline from Mozambique serve a regional market too small to justify a rival complex of that size.
Sasol is an incumbent defending a carbon-intensive model; no rival is held back from copying a new Sasol business model.

Sasol has run Fischer-Tropsch synthesis at industrial scale for decades and its technology underpins the Oryx GTL plant in Qatar (a joint venture with QatarEnergy) and its ecoFT sustainable-fuel plans.

It owns captive coal mines feeding Secunda and holds Mozambican gas rights (Pande-Temane), though Mozambican gas is depleting and Sasol impaired its Mozambique Production Sharing Agreement by R3.8bn in FY2026.

customers.evidence: Sasol does not publish retention or NPS; fuel sales volumes rose to 57.5 mm bbl in FY2026 from 50.9 mm bbl, and chemical sales volumes rose in Africa (3,542 kt) and America (1,904 kt), but customers buy largely on price.

talent.evidence: With 27,239 employees at 30 June 2026, Sasol is a major South African employer of chemical engineers and runs long-standing bursary programmes, but it does not feature in global best-employer rankings and has had repeated restructurings and two workplace fatalities in FY2026.

product.evidence: Its Fischer-Tropsch fuels and chemicals are technically distinctive (e.g. waxes and alcohols from Secunda and Germany), but most products are commodities and the US Lake Charles complex has needed large impairments.

competitors.name: TotalEnergies SE
competitors.note: Competes in South African fuel retail and is Sasol's partner in the Natref refinery; also a global chemicals producer.

competitors.name: Shell plc
competitors.note: Fuel retail in South Africa, gas-to-liquids (Pearl GTL) and detergent alcohols/chemicals.

competitors.name: BP p.l.c.
competitors.note: Fuel retail and commercial fuels in South Africa.

competitors.name: Astron Energy (Glencore plc)
competitors.note: Owns the Cape Town refinery and Caltex-branded fuel stations in South Africa.

competitors.name: Engen (Vivo Energy)
competitors.note: Large South African fuel retail network and fuel imports.

competitors.name: Dow Inc.
competitors.note: Ethylene, polyethylene, alcohols and surfactant intermediates in the US and Europe.

competitors.name: LyondellBasell Industries N.V.
competitors.note: US Gulf Coast ethylene and polymers, competing with Sasol's Lake Charles complex.

competitors.name: BASF SE
competitors.note: Surfactants, alcohols and specialty chemicals in Europe and globally.

competitors.name: INEOS
competitors.note: Olefins, polymers and alpha olefins in Europe and the US.

competitors.name: Exxon Mobil (ExxonMobil Holdings Corporation)
competitors.note: Global chemicals (polymers, specialty fluids) and fuels.

competitors.name: SABIC
competitors.note: Polymers and base chemicals sold into Africa, Europe and Asia.

competitors.name: Omnia Holdings
competitors.note: Fertilisers and mining explosives in Southern Africa.

competitors.name: Wilmar International
competitors.note: Oleochemical (palm-based) alcohols competing with Sasol's synthetic alcohols.

threats: South Africa's carbon tax, Minimum Emission Standards and its own 30% emissions-reduction target by 2030 could force costly cuts to Secunda output.
Mozambican gas from Pande-Temane is depleting, threatening gas feedstock for Secunda and Sasolburg and supply to South African industry (R3.8bn Mozambique PSA impairment in FY2026).
Earnings swing with Brent oil, refining margins, chemical prices and the rand; FY2026 benefited from a Middle East conflict and Strait of Hormuz closure that may not last.
Repeated impairments of the Secunda liquid-fuels refinery (R7.7bn in FY2026) and US/polyethylene assets (R3.7bn) point to weak returns on capital.
Net debt of US$3.3bn is still above the US$3bn level needed to restart dividends.
Electric vehicles and lower-carbon fuels could shrink long-term demand for liquid fuels.
Weak South African logistics (Transnet rail and ports) and coal quality issues have disrupted volumes in past years.

ceo.name: Simon Baloyi
ceo.background: Chemical engineer with Master's degrees in Engineering Management and Chemical Engineering; joined Sasol in 2002 and was EVP Energy Operations and Technology before becoming President and CEO on 1 April 2024.

c1.evidence: Sasol is a mature coal- and gas-based fuels and chemicals producer, not the leader of a young fast-growing industry; turnover of R272,118m in FY2026 was below FY2023's R289,696m.

c2.evidence: Customers choose Sasol mainly for local availability and integrated supply from Secunda and the Mozambique gas pipeline, an asset-based edge that is hard to copy but tied to depleting gas and carbon-heavy coal.

c3.evidence: Sasol is a household name in South Africa (fuel stations, Secunda) and one of the JSE's largest industrial companies, but it is little known to ordinary consumers elsewhere and is not a default global leader.

c4.evidence: Its stated purpose is 'Innovating for a better world' with a 2050 net-zero ambition and 2,000 MW of renewables targeted by 2030, but management's focus in FY2026 was cutting costs and net debt to restart dividends.

c6.evidence: “South African, coal-to-fuel, polluter, cyclical” – the impression is mixed: respected as a national industrial champion and engineering employer, but widely criticised for Secunda's carbon emissions and for repeated impairments and shareholder losses.

c7.evidence: Its main markets, South African liquid fuels and commodity chemicals, are large but mature and face a secular shift away from fossil fuels.

c8.evidence: Fischer-Tropsch know-how could be applied to sustainable aviation fuel and green-hydrogen-based fuels through Sasol ecoFT, but these remain early and unproven at scale.

m1.evidence: Simon Baloyi has set out a plan to reset Secunda, lift International Chemicals and transition to lower-carbon feedstocks, but it is a practical turnaround plan rather than a bold vision of the future.

m2.evidence: Baloyi is a 2002-joined Sasol lifer, not a founder; his focus on balance sheet repair and long-term feedstock security shows long-term thinking within a professional-manager role.

m4.evidence: Baloyi stresses that 'Safety remains our foremost priority' and Sasol's values start with 'Be safe' and 'Be caring', but there is little independent evidence of a distinctive servant-leadership style.

m5.evidence: Sasol's culture is engineering- and safety-focused, but recent years have been about cost cutting (cash fixed costs held flat at about R70bn for three years) rather than a stream of new products.

m6.evidence: Baloyi holds Master's degrees in Chemical Engineering and Engineering Management and ran Sasol's Energy Operations and Technology division before becoming CEO.

m7.evidence: There is no public controversy about Baloyi's character, but also little evidence beyond standard corporate statements to judge whether his stewardship aims at something bigger than profit.

m7b.evidence: No record was found of Simon Baloyi giving a commencement speech at a top university.

m8b.evidence: Baloyi has a low-key, technical public profile rather than a distinctive, memorable personality.

m9.evidence: Since April 2024 he has met FY2026 Capital Markets Day targets (Secunda output up 8% to 7.26 mt, net debt down 11% to US$3.3bn, adjusted EBITDA up 17% to about R61bn), but the group still booked R16.8bn of impairments and has not restored a dividend.

m10.evidence: Sasol has held group cash fixed costs flat at about R70bn for three consecutive years and cut capital expenditure 18% to about R21bn in FY2026, though this is cost discipline from necessity rather than a famed frugal culture.

c10.evidence: Its fuels, fertilisers, explosives and chemicals are essential inputs for South Africa's economy and for global consumer goods makers, but they are commodity inputs rather than life-changing products for billions of people.

p2.evidence: Running coal- and gas-to-liquids Fischer-Tropsch plants at Secunda's scale is technically very hard and important for South Africa's fuel security, though the technology is mature and carbon-intensive.

f1.evidence: Turnover rose in FY2022 (R272,746m) and FY2023 (R289,696m) but fell in FY2024 (R275,111m) and FY2025 (R249,096m) before recovering to R272,118m in FY2026.

f2.evidence: Operating profit before remeasurement items fell from 19.1% of turnover in FY2023 (R55,418m) to 15.8% in FY2026 (R43,010m), and Sasol does not report a gross margin.

f3.evidence: Equity is positive at R170,034m, but debt of R95,276m (long-term R67,874m plus short-term R27,402m, excluding leases) far exceeds cash of R43,304m at 30 June 2026.

f4.evidence: Operating profit before remeasurement items moved from R39,837m in FY2021 to R43,010m in FY2026 after peaking at R55,418m in FY2023, and cash generated by operating activities fell from R64,637m in FY2023 to R41,970m in FY2026.

v1.evidence: Sasol's fuels and most chemicals are interchangeable commodities; there is no simple reason an ordinary buyer would pick them over rivals' products.

v2.evidence: No evidence was found of Sasol appearing in major global best-places-to-work rankings; it is a respected local employer of engineers but has cut jobs and suffered two fatalities in FY2026.

c5.evidence: If Sasol disappeared, South Africa would lose a large share of its domestic fuel, much of its industrial gas and many chemical inputs, causing real shortages, though the world outside Southern Africa would barely notice.
